analysis.one_liner: Puts the unregulated over-the-counter derivatives market under federal oversight with clearing, reporting, capital, and anti-manipulation rules.
analysis.headline: Sen. Jack Reed's bill to regulate the swaps market drew no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a vote or a committee hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the special exemption, written into law in 2000, that kept most over-the-counter derivatives — the private contracts between banks and big investors that helped trigger the 2008 financial crisis — outside federal oversight. It required standardized swaps to be cleared through regulated central counterparties or reported to trade repositories so regulators and the public could see who held what, required big derivatives dealers to register with the SEC or CFTC and hold minimum capital and margin, banned fraud and manipulation in the swaps market, and directed regulators to set position limits to curb excessive speculation. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary savers, workers whose pensions and 401(k)s are tied to financial markets, and taxpayers who otherwise absorb the cost of bailouts when hidden derivatives bets go bad. The bill's own findings state that unregulated derivatives risk-taking was a significant cause of the financial crisis [S3]. Businesses and municipalities that use swaps to hedge real risks would also gain from more transparent pricing and stronger protections against being sold unsuitable products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Savers, pension holders, taxpayers, swap end users

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exclusion of swap agreements from regulatory oversight under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and the Commodity Futures Modernization Act, bringing a market that had operated outside federal supervision back under the law.

Requires standardized security-based and commodity-based swaps to be cleared through registered clearing agencies or reported to registered trade repositories, and directs regulators to collect and publish transaction data, so regulators, investors, and the public can see who holds what.

Requires significant derivatives market participants to register with the SEC or CFTC and meet capital and margin requirements, with recordkeeping and reporting duties, so dealers can absorb their own losses instead of passing them on.
Prohibits fraudulent, deceptive, or manipulative practices in swaps markets and directs the SEC to set position limits, and revises restrictions on excessive speculation in commodity markets.
Adds business-conduct rules requiring dealers to disclose risks, fees, and conflicts of interest to counterparties, and to assess whether a swap is appropriate for the buyer.

analysis.who_pays: The large banks and dealers that dominated the opaque over-the-counter swaps market would bear registration, capital, margin, clearing, and reporting costs, and lose profits that came from trading outside oversight. Some of those costs would be passed through to end users that hedge legitimate business risks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big bank derivatives dealers and swap traders

drawbacks.text: Capital, margin, clearing, and exchange-trading requirements raise the cost of using swaps, and dealers would pass some of that on to businesses hedging real risks — airlines fuel costs, manufacturers' currency exposure, municipal issuers' borrowing costs — and possibly to their customers.

The bill divides authority over derivatives among four sets of regulators — the SEC, the CFTC, federal banking agencies, and the FHFA — which could produce overlapping rules in some areas and gaps in others.

Concentrating standardized swaps in central counterparties makes those clearinghouses a potential single point of failure; the bill itself directs regulators to impose risk-management controls on them to make sure they can meet settlement obligations, an acknowledgment of the risk the structure creates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits and costs are unevenly matched: the market being regulated was, per the bill's own findings, a significant cause of the 2008 crisis, and the main costs fall on the largest dealers, with a smaller pass-through to legitimate hedgers. The design is reasonable but not clean — four regulators sharing jurisdiction invites gaps, and the clearing mandate trades dealer opacity for concentration risk at clearinghouses. On balance the transparency and capital rules address a real, documented danger to the whole economy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the Congress ended with it still in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on September 22, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No other member of the Senate signed on; the bill had zero cosponsors.
The action history ends with the committee referral; no further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
The bill never reached the Senate floor and no roll-call vote was ever held on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks and dealers trading swaps outside federal oversight stayed unregulated — though the core of this proposal was not lost for long: Congress passed comprehensive derivatives regulation a few months later as part of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform Act of 2010, so the dealers ultimately did face these rules even though this particular bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unregulated dealers — until similar rules passed in 2010

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Comprehensive Derivatives Regulation Act of 2009 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled in the 111th Congress.

against.name: Wall Street banks and derivatives dealers
against.role: The dominant dealers in the unregulated over-the-counter swaps market
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive derivatives regulation during the 2009-2010 financial reform debate, lobbying against mandatory clearing, exchange trading, and capital requirements on their swap businesses.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party and no roll call, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the larger fight over derivatives rules that later became law in Dodd-Frank split mainly on party lines.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 2000-law exclusions that kept their over-the-counter swap businesses outside federal oversight, and imposes registration, capital, margin, clearing, reporting, and anti-fraud rules. Their profits in this market came substantially from its opacity and lack of regulation, which is exactly what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Derivatives clearinghouses, exchanges, and trade repositories
industries.note: The bill makes registered clearing agencies and trade repositories the mandatory channel for standardized swaps and creates registration and business for swap execution facilities. That gives them a permanent gatekeeper role and a captive fee stream, even though the mandate serves public transparency and stability.

industries.industry: Corporate and municipal swap end users
industries.note: Businesses, pension plans, and municipalities that use swaps to hedge genuine risks gain disclosure protections, fairer pricing, and conflict-of-interest rules, but face margin, clearing, and exchange-trading requirements that raise hedging costs.

Registration, capital, margin, and position-limit rules cover significant market participants trading for their own accounts, restricting large speculative positions and speculative activity in commodity markets.
